t: let me put to [the] test/ you

x.ASV: I said in my heart, Come now, I will prove thee with mirth; therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also was vanity.
x.Darby: I said in my heart, Come now, I will try thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure. But behold, this also is vanity.
x.KJV: I said in mine heart, Go to now, I will prove thee with mirth, therefore enjoy pleasure: and, behold, this also is vanity.
x.YLT: I said in my heart, `Pray, come, I try thee with mirth, and look thou on gladness;' and lo, even it is vanity.

nt: Qoheleth is speaking of his own thoughts as if they were a person that he could talk to, his **heart**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I thought to myself]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **joy**, you could express that idea in another way. Also, Qoheleth is speaking of **good** as if it were a thing that he could **see**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by making you glad and letting you experience what is pleasant]
Qoheleth is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. See how you translated this word in [1:14](../01/14.md).
See how you translated this word in [1:14](../01/14.md).

x.ASV: I said of laughter, It is mad; and of mirth, What doeth it?
x.Darby: I said of laughter, Madness! and of mirth, What availeth it?
x.KJV: I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?
x.YLT: Of laughter I said, `Foolish!' and of mirth, `What is this it is doing?'

nt: Qoheleth is speaking **To laughter** and **to joy** though he knows they cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening that he feels very strongly about these emotions and their place in life. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about them. Alternate translation: [About laughter, I said, “Madness!” And about joy]

Qoheleth is using a word that expresses a strong feeling of scorn. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Ridiculous]

Qoheleth is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [And to joy, I said, “What is this doing]

Qoheleth is using the question form to show that pleasure accomplishes nothing worthwhile. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [This accomplishes nothing!]

x.ASV: I searched in my heart how to cheer my flesh with wine, my heart yet guiding me with wisdom, and how to lay hold on folly, till I might see what it was good for the sons of men that they should do under heaven all the days of their life.
x.Darby: I searched in my heart how to cherish my flesh with wine, while practising my heart with wisdom; and how to lay hold on folly, till I should see what was that good for the children of men which they should do under the heavens all the days of their life.
x.KJV: I sought in mine heart to give myself unto wine, yet acquainting mine heart with wisdom; and to lay hold on folly, till I might see what was that good for the sons of men, which they should do under the heaven all the days of their life.
x.YLT: I have sought in my heart to draw out with wine my appetite, (and my heart leading in wisdom), and to take hold on folly till that I see where is this--the good to the sons of man of that which they do under the heavens, the number of the days of their lives.

nt: Qoheleth is using **to drag my flesh with wine** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to gratify my body with wine.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to gratify my body with wine]

Qoheleth is speaking of his **heart** as if it were a living thing that could guide him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I was still thinking wisely all the while]

Qoheleth is speaking of **folly** as if it were an object that he could take hold of with his hand. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and to take up foolish behavior]

Here the masculine term **sons** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. See how you translated the same phrase in [1:13](../01/13.md).

Qoheleth is using **under the heavens** as a common expression of the culture to mean “here on the earth during this life.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. See how you translated the similar phrase in [1:3](.../01/03.md) Alternate translation: [here on the earth]

x.ASV: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards;
x.Darby: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards;
x.KJV: I made me great works; I builded me houses; I planted me vineyards:
x.YLT: I made great my works, I builded for me houses, I planted for me vineyards.

nt: בָּנִ֤יתִי לִ⁠י֙ בָּתִּ֔ים נָטַ֥עְתִּי לִ֖⁠י כְּרָמִֽים

Qoheleth is using **I built for myself houses** and **I planted for myself vineyards** to represent the work that he had others do for him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I had houses built for myself. I had vineyards planted for myself]

x.ASV: I made me gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of all kinds of fruit;
x.Darby: I made me gardens and parks, and I planted trees in them of every kind of fruit;
x.KJV: I made me gardens and orchards, and I planted trees in them of all kind of fruits:
x.YLT: I made for me gardens and paradises, and I planted in them trees of every fruit.

nt: The term **royal parks** describes large, enclosed gardens that belonged to a king. If your readers would not be familiar with what royal parks are, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and large walled gardens]

Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe a **tree** that is characterized by the kind of **fruit** that it bears. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [every kind of fruit tree]

x.ASV: I made me pools of water, to water therefrom the forest where trees were reared;
x.Darby: I made me ponds of water, to water therewith the wood, where the trees are reared.
x.KJV: I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees:
x.YLT: I made for me pools of water, to water from them a forest shooting forth trees.

x.ASV: I bought men-servants and maid-servants, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all that were before me in Jerusalem;
x.Darby: I acquired servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of herds and flocks, above all that had been in Jerusalem before me.
x.KJV: I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me:
x.YLT: I got men-servants, and maid-servants, and sons of the house were to me; also, I had much substance--herd and flock--above all who had been before me in Jerusalem.

nt: Qoheleth is using **sons of the house** as a common expression of the culture to mean “servants who were born in my household.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and servants born in my household]

Here the expression **to my face** means “before me” (in time). If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [before me]

x.ASV: I gathered me also silver and gold, and the treasure of kings and of the provinces; I gat me men-singers and women-singers, and the delights of the sons of men, musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
x.Darby: I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces; I got me men-singers and women-singers, and the delights of the children of men, a wife and concubines.
x.KJV: I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts.
x.YLT: I gathered for me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces. I prepared for me men-singers and women-singers, and the luxuries of the sons of man--a wife and wives.

nt: Qoheleth is using the possessive form to describe **treasure** that is characterized by belonging to **kings and provinces**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the treasure that kings and provinces possessed]

Qoheleth is using **breast and breasts** to represent women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [an abundance of women] or [many women for myself]

x.ASV: So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me.
x.Darby: And I became great, and increased more than all that had been before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me.
x.KJV: So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me.
x.YLT: And I became great, and increased above every one who had been before me in Jerusalem; also, my wisdom stood with me.

nt: Qoheleth is speaking of his **wisdom** as if it were a living thing that could stand beside him as a companion. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I remained wise through it all]

x.ASV: And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them; I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced because of all my labor; and this was my portion from all my labor.
x.Darby: And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them: I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour, and this was my portion from all my labour.
x.KJV: And whatsoever mine eyes desired I kept not from them, I withheld not my heart from any joy; for my heart rejoiced in all my labour: and this was my portion of all my labour.
x.YLT: And all that mine eyes asked I kept not back from them; I withheld not my heart from any joy, for my heart rejoiced because of all my labour, and this hath been my portion, from all my labour,

nt: Qoheleth is speaking of the enjoyment that he received from his work as if it were a **portion** of land or food that had been assigned to him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and this was what I received in return for all my toil]

x.ASV: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labor that I had labored to do; and, behold, all was vanity and a striving after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
x.Darby: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that it had cost me to do [them]; and behold, all was vanity and pursuit of the wind, and there was no profit under the sun.
x.KJV: Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do: and, behold, all was vanity and vexation of spirit, and there was no profit under the sun.
x.YLT: and I have looked on all my works that my hands have done, and on the labour that I have laboured to do, and lo, the whole is vanity and vexation of spirit, and there is no advantage under the sun!

nt: Here, **my hands** represents my own efforts. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [that I had accomplished by my own efforts]

Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of expressing this. Alternate translation: [and to the work that I had labored to accomplish]
See how you translated the same expression in [1:14](../01/14.md).
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **profit**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and nothing under the sun benefited me]

x.ASV: And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly: for what can the man do that cometh after the king? even that which hath been done long ago.
x.Darby: And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly; for what shall the man [do] that cometh after the king? — that which hath already been done.
x.KJV: And I turned myself to behold wisdom, and madness, and folly: for what can the man do that cometh after the king? even that which hath been already done.
x.YLT: And I turned to see wisdom, and madness, and folly, but what is the man who cometh after the king? that which is already--they have done it!

nt: מֶ֣ה הָ⁠אָדָ֗ם שֶׁ⁠יָּבוֹא֙ אַחֲרֵ֣י הַ⁠מֶּ֔לֶךְ אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר כְּבָ֖ר עָשֽׂוּ⁠הוּ

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that whoever comes after him will not be able to do anything more than what has already been done. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [the person who will come after the king can do nothing more than what has already been done.]

Qoheleth is not referring to a specific **person**. He means people in general who might come after him. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [what can any person do who will come after the king]
Qoheleth is speaking of himself in the third person as **the king**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [after me]

x.ASV: Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.
x.Darby: And I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as light excelleth darkness.
x.KJV: Then I saw that wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness.
x.YLT: And I saw that there is an advantage to wisdom above folly, like the advantage of the light above the darkness.

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **the light** is more useful than **the darkness** for seeing where one is going, so wisdom is more useful than folly for living well. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as light helps a person to see where he is going, but darkness does not]

x.ASV: The wise man’s eyes are in his head, and the fool walketh in darkness: and yet I perceived that one event happeneth to them all.
x.Darby: The wise man's eyes are in his head, and the fool walketh in darkness; but I myself also perceived that one event happeneth to them all.
x.KJV: The wise man’s eyes are in his head; but the fool walketh in darkness: and I myself perceived also that one event happeneth to them all.
x.YLT: The wise! --his eyes are in his head, and the fool in darkness is walking, and I also knew that one event happeneth with them all;

nt: Qoheleth is using the expression that **his eyes are in his head** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he sees where he is going.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The wise, he sees where he is going]

Qoheleth is speaking of the way a foolish person lives as if it were **walking** in **the darkness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but the fool lives without understanding]

Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its subject come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. The implication is that the one **happening** that will happen to both of them is death. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternatively, your language may have another way of expressing this. Alternate translation: [that the same thing will occur to both of them] or [that one thing, namely death, will happen to both of them]

x.ASV: Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so will it happen even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then said I in my heart, that this also is vanity.
x.Darby: And I said in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool so will it happen even to me; and why was I then so wise? Then I said in my heart that this also is vanity.
x.KJV: Then said I in my heart, As it happeneth to the fool, so it happeneth even to me; and why was I then more wise? Then I said in my heart, that this also is vanity.
x.YLT: and I said in my heart, `As it happeneth with the fool, it happeneth also with me, and why am I then more wise?' And I spake in my heart, that also this is vanity:

nt: Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of dismay. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Alas, the very thing that happens to the fool will happen to me too]

Qoheleth is using the question form to express his frustration that becoming **wise** gained him no lasting advantage. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And so I was exceedingly wise for no reason at all!]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as a direct quotation. Alternate translation: [And I said to my heart, “This also is vapor.”]

x.ASV: For of the wise man, even as of the fool, there is no remembrance for ever; seeing that in the days to come all will have been long forgotten. And how doth the wise man die even as the fool!
x.Darby: For there shall be no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; because everything is already forgotten in the days which come. And how dieth the wise even as the fool?
x.KJV: For there is no remembrance of the wise more than of the fool for ever; seeing that which now is in the days to come shall all be forgotten. And how dieth the wise man? as the fool.
x.YLT: That there is no remembrance to the wise--with the fool--to the age, for that which is already, in the days that are coming is all forgotten, and how dieth the wise? with the fool!

nt: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **memory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people do not remember the wise person]

The expression **forgotten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one will remember either of them]

Qoheleth is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of grief. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible! The wise die with the fool]

x.ASV: So I hated life, because the work that is wrought under the sun was grievous unto me; for all is vanity and a striving after wind.
x.Darby: And I hated life; for the work that is wrought under the sun was grievous unto me; for all is vanity and pursuit of the wind.
x.KJV: Therefore I hated life; because the work that is wrought under the sun is grievous unto me: for all is vanity and vexation of spirit.
x.YLT: And I have hated life, for sad to me is the work that hath been done under the sun, for the whole is vanity and vexation of spirit.

nt: The expression **was done** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [was the work that people did under the sun]

x.ASV: And I hated all my labor wherein I labored under the sun, seeing that I must leave it unto the man that shall be after me.
x.Darby: And I hated all my labour wherewith I had been toiling under the sun, because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me.
x.KJV: Yea, I hated all my labour which I had taken under the sun: because I should leave it unto the man that shall be after me.
x.YLT: And I have hated all my labour that I labour at under the sun, because I leave it to a man who is after me.

nt: אֶת כָּל עֲמָלִ֔⁠י שֶׁ⁠אֲנִ֥י עָמֵ֖ל תַּ֣חַת הַ⁠שָּׁ֑מֶשׁ

Here, **my toil** represents what I had gained by my toil. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the possessions that I had earned by my hard work under the sun]

x.ASV: And who knoweth whether he will be a wise man or a fool? yet will he have rule over all my labor wherein I have labored, and wherein I have showed myself wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
x.Darby: And who knoweth whether he will be a wise [man] or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour at which I have laboured, and wherein I have been wise under the sun. This also is vanity.
x.KJV: And who knoweth whether he shall be a wise man or a fool? yet shall he have rule over all my labour wherein I have laboured, and wherein I have shewed myself wise under the sun. This is also vanity.
x.YLT: And who knoweth whether he is wise or foolish? yet he doth rule over all my labour that I have laboured at, and that I have done wisely under the sun! this also is vanity.

nt: וּ⁠מִ֣י יוֹדֵ֗עַ הֶֽ⁠חָכָ֤ם יִהְיֶה֙ א֣וֹ סָכָ֔ל

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to know the answer. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [And no one knows whether he will be wise or a fool.]

The pronoun **he** refers to the person who will come after Qoheleth, whom he mentions at the end of the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Will that person who comes after me be wise or a fool]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **authority**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And he will rule over all my toil]

x.ASV: Therefore I turned about to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labor wherein I had labored under the sun.
x.Darby: Then I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour wherewith I had laboured under the sun.
x.KJV: Therefore I went about to cause my heart to despair of all the labour which I took under the sun.
x.YLT: And I turned round to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labour that I laboured at under the sun.

x.ASV: For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, and with knowledge, and with skilfulness; yet to a man that hath not labored therein shall he leave it for his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil.
x.Darby: For there is a man whose labour hath been with wisdom, and with knowledge, and with skill, and who leaveth it to a man that hath not laboured therein, to be his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil.
x.KJV: For there is a man whose labour is in wisdom, and in knowledge, and in equity; yet to a man that hath not laboured therein shall he leave it for his portion. This also is vanity and a great evil.
x.YLT: For there is a man whose labour is in wisdom, and in knowledge, and in equity, and to a man who hath not laboured therein he giveth it--his portion! Even this is vanity and a great evil.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **wisdom** and **knowledge** and **skill**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [is that of someone who is wise, knows much, and who possesses skills]

x.ASV: For what hath a man of all his labor, and of the striving of his heart, wherein he laboreth under the sun?
x.Darby: For what will man have of all his labour and of the striving of his heart, wherewith he hath wearied himself under the sun?
x.KJV: For what hath man of all his labour, and of the vexation of his heart, wherein he hath laboured under the sun?
x.YLT: For what hath been to a man by all his labour, and by the thought of his heart that he laboured at under the sun?

nt: כִּ֠י מֶֽה הֹוֶ֤ה לָֽ⁠אָדָם֙ בְּ⁠כָל עֲמָל֔⁠וֹ וּ⁠בְ⁠רַעְי֖וֹן לִבּ֑⁠ו שֶׁ⁠ה֥וּא עָמֵ֖ל תַּ֥חַת הַ⁠שָּֽׁמֶשׁ

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that nothing lasting comes to a person from all his hard work. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [For nothing endures for the person in exchange for all his toil and the striving of his heart with which he labors under the sun.]

x.ASV: For all his days are but sorrows, and his travail is grief; yea, even in the night his heart taketh no rest. This also is vanity.
x.Darby: For all his days are sorrows, and his travail vexation: even in the night his heart taketh no rest. This also is vanity.
x.KJV: For all his days are sorrows, and his travail grief; yea, his heart taketh not rest in the night. This is also vanity.
x.YLT: For all his days are sorrows, and his travail sadness; even at night his heart hath not lain down; this also is vanity.

nt: Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s **days** as if they were **pains** and of his **anger** as if it were **business**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [all his days are full of pain, and his work causes him grief]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **anger** and **business**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [and he works angrily]

x.ASV: There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labor. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
x.Darby: There is nothing good for man, but that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand ofGod.
x.KJV: There is nothing better for a man, than that he should eat and drink, and that he should make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it was from the hand of God.
x.YLT: There is nothing good in a man who eateth, and hath drunk, and hath shewn his soul good in his labour. This also I have seen that it is from the hand of God.

nt: Here the masculine term **he** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [There is nothing better for humanity than that he or she should eat and drink]

Qoheleth is using **cause his spirit to see good** as a common expression of the culture to mean “find enjoyment.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and enjoy himself in his toil]
Here, **the hand of the God** represents what God gives. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [is what God gives]

x.ASV: For who can eat, or who can have enjoyment, more than I?
x.Darby: For who can eat, or who be eager, more than I?
x.KJV: For who can eat, or who else can hasten hereunto, more than I?
x.YLT: For who eateth and who hasteth out more than I?

nt: כִּ֣י מִ֥י יֹאכַ֛ל וּ⁠מִ֥י יָח֖וּשׁ ח֥וּץ מִמֶּֽ⁠נִּי

Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to eat or to enjoy anything apart from God. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [for no one can eat or enjoy anything apart from him!]

Some ancient manuscripts read “apart from him.” The ULT follows that reading. Other ancient manuscripts read “apart from me.” If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT.

x.Darby: For he giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy; but to the sinner he giveth travail to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good inGod's sight. This also is vanity and pursuit of the wind.
x.KJV: For God giveth to a man that is good in his sight wisdom, and knowledge, and joy: but to the sinner he giveth travail, to gather and to heap up, that he may give to him that is good before God. This also is vanity and vexation of spirit.

nt: Here, **to his face** represents in his judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [who is good in his judgment]
The pronoun **he** refers to God, whom Qoheleth names later in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy]

The terms **gathering** and **collecting** mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [of amassing wealth]
